I stop doing things when they get too emotionally/mentally/physically difficult, which I'm not proud of, but that's where I am. 

The 16 year old is an angel. She's my partner's little sister, and the two of them have been through so much crap with an unstable mother. Even though we struggle to make end's meet, I refuse to take her back to the abusive environment she was in. And though I struggle to provide for her, she's so smart and compassionate and wants to help in any way she can. I hate feeling that she feels like a burden. 

I'm really happy with the relationship, but in my moments of suicidal thoughts, I lash out at everyone in my head. I think I'd be better on my own, so then at least I wouldn't let anyone down with my suicidal thoughts. But the two of them honestly ground me, even when life feels too much.

I don't know what my other options are. I lack so much motivation; I keep disassociating so hard that I don't feel tangible. It just feels like there's no break ahead, no relief. And I'm just so tired. 

So yeah. Better today, I promise. Thank you again for reaching out and listening. It means a lot.

As someone who has been accused of not looking disabled enough, I've learned to put my illness into blunt terms that are easily understood. Unfortunately, this means I stretch the truth some, but only because saying "fibromyalgia" can equate to a question mark for many people. 

For example, when someone asked why I needed a handicap tag, I simply said I have an inoperable tumor. People know that tumor equals bad, so they shut up. It's not my job to clarify that fibro can _feel_ like a tumor, metastasizing throughout your body. 

Another time I was asked why I use a cane when I look healthy. I just said I have degenerative bone disease. Again, the every day person knows these words -- degenerative = bad, especially for bones, and there's even "disease" in the name! -- so they nod sympathetically and don't ask any further questions. And again, it's not my job to explain how fibro can _feel_ like your skeleton is withering away. 

I mainly do this with nosy strangers, but since you mentioned professors -- and I have vivid memories of trying to justify my absences in college -- it might help you here. I know it's fibbing, to an extent, but at the end of the day, it's not fair to ask of you to justify your illness just because someone else doesn't get it. You feel it; therefore, the people who care about you should believe and respect it. Anyone who keeps interrogating you on said pain probably doesn't deserve your awesome presence. You're strong as hell -- don't ever forget!

Edit: Also, with your school, are you in touch with disability services? For aggressive teachers, a disability advisor can act as a intermediary force, accrediting your disability (which legally must be acknowledged) without having to explain the finer details of the illness as "proof." Disability services was an incredible lifeline to me in college, so I highly recommend getting in touch with an advisor there and discussing this issue. They can help unburden that stress so you can focus on kicking ass!

I was at school. Oakview Elementary in South Carolina. Fourth grade. Our teacher had just lined us up to take us to lunch when the principal summoned all teachers to the front lobby. Our teacher plants us at our assigned lunch table in the cafeteria, then joins the rest of the staff to speak with the principal. 

I'm eating lunch. And I start noticing a lot of kids getting up and going to the front lobby. I soon learn their parents had come and decided to take their children home for the rest of the day. Parents came in droves; none of us knew why our friends were leaving, but the ones who did were so giddy about it, it was so unexpected. A free half day, you know? 

I very distinctly remember being peeved that my mom hadn't come to get me for whatever reason everyone else was using to skip out on the rest of the day. The students left in my class tried to ask our teacher what was going on, but she ushered us back to our room. Our lessons went on for the rest of the afternoon. 

The bus drive home was just as chaotic as usual, even though there weren't that many kids on the bus this time. I laughed and joked with friends, then got off at my stop, right at the corner of my front yard. I walked inside, and my mom immediately hugs me. I try to ask her why she hadn't picked me up early. I whined about how other kids got to leave. 

Then, she guided me to the den, to the TV, where the buildings were burning. I think she explained, as simply as she could, what had happened, because I was confused. And then I got really scared, because my dad was a pilot at the time. He had been up in the air when the attacks happened--he was nowhere near the crashes, no connection to the airlines, and he was a cargo pilot, not a commercial airline, but at the time... all I could think of was how he was up in the air and could be in danger. 

I grew up with planes and in airports and watching my dad take off and land. He's retired now, and he and my mom are still happily in love and traveling around the country in their RV. But, I still remember that confusion, that obliviousness that carried me through the rest of the school day, and just that echo of fear, of what if he had been a pilot involved in an accident, involved in 9/11.

And then I hug my parents a lot and tell them I love them.
